notes.body:
There is a hidden order in this list, and once we catch it the whole week opens like a lock. Each day is tied to its meaning by the **number folded inside its own Arabic name**, and the count climbs steadily from rest toward gathering.

Saturday (السبت) is named from ceasing and stillness, so it is given to repose. Sunday (الأحد) carries the word for one, so it holds unity and the single turning of the year. From there the numbers take over:

1. Monday (الاثنين) is two, the day of the doublings.
2. Tuesday (الثلاثاء) is three, given three houses.
3. Wednesday (الأربعاء) is four, given the four sacred things.
4. Thursday (الخميس) is five, given the fifth of the causes of Allah.

Friday (الجمعة) is named from gathering, and so it is the greatest law — the day that draws all the others into one.

Now the terms the chapter leaves unspoken. The doublings (التثنية) are the great **Pair** — not two separate things, but one origin folded into two, the way every rank in creation descends from a first couple. Tuesday's three houses are the three tiers this chapter later unveils: the outward (الظاهر), the inward (الباطن), and the inmost (باطن الباطن) — the shell, the white, and the yolk of the guarded egg. The four sacred things are the four sacred months (الأشهر الحرم) that Allah set apart from the twelve months of the year, withdrawn from ordinary time.

Al-Tawbah 9:36

And the fifth of the causes of Allah is the fifth rank among the causes — those luminous intermediaries the chapter names as standing between Allah and His Speakers, counted here to five as a day of five would ask. So nothing in the list is idle: each day's name announces its number, and the number summons its own sacred set.
notes.anchor: Monday is for the doublings, in the great meaning
notes.quote: Monday is for the doublings, in the great meaning
etymology: السبت (the Sabbath): from the root س-ب-ت, to cut off and come to rest. The week's labour is severed and stillness is what remains — which is why the first day answers to repose rather than to any number in its name.

الاثنين (Monday): from the root ث-ن-ي, to fold one thing back upon another. The same root yields the doublings (التثنية) — not two separate things but one turned into a pair, so the day of two becomes the day of the great Pair.

الحرم (the sacred): from the root ح-ر-م, to forbid and set apart. What is sacred is precisely what is fenced off from common use, so the four sacred things (الأشهر الحرم) are the four spans of time withdrawn from the ordinary year.

الجمعة (Friday): from the root ج-م-ع, to gather and bring together. The day of congregation pulls the scattered worshippers into a single body — which is why it stands as the greatest law, the day that gathers all the rest into itself.

notes.body:
### The seven and the two, and why they sit highest

When the boy asks about the seven kingdoms of the heavens and their orbits, the Master answers with a count that seems not to add up: **"the seven and the two orbits."** He is naming the whole visible order of the sky — the seven turning spheres we track by the wandering stars الكواكب السيّارة, and above them two greater orbits that carry everything else and enclose the seven within them.

Picture our sky as a set of nested glass globes. The inner seven move in plain view; but they all ride inside two vast outer shells — the sphere that holds the fixed stars الكواكب الثابتة, and the outermost orbit that turns the entire heavens once each day. Those two are counted apart because they do not merely move among the rest — **they contain the rest**, and to contain a thing is to stand higher than it.

### Why these are the greatest causes

In this teaching a cause (سبب) is a rung on the ladder between Allah and His creation, and **rank on that ladder is everything**. The seven-and-two belong to the Speaking Imam النّاطق, who stands at the summit of the earthly order. Their height in the sky is a likeness of his height among people: as the two great orbits gather all the lower spheres inside them, the Speaker gathers all the rulings and all the ranks beneath him.

### How the seven seas differ

The seven seas are also called causes, and the boy is right to hear the echo — but the Master sets them "below those first causes." The heavens are above; the seas rest upon the earth. So the heavens are the causes tying Allah to the Speaker, while **the seas are the causes tying Allah to the imams who come after him**. The difference is not the number seven; it is the level. Height in the world of nature mirrors nearness in the world of rank, and the imam stands one degree below the Speaker exactly as the sea lies one world below the sky.
notes.anchor: These are the seven and the two orbits
notes.quote: These are the seven and the two orbits
etymology: سبب (cause): from the root س-ب-ب, whose first sense is a rope or cord — the one let down to reach water in a well, or gripped to climb. A سبب is therefore a means or link by which a far thing is reached, here a rung connecting the creation upward toward Allah.

النّاطق (the Speaker): from the root ن-ط-ق, to utter articulate speech. The نَاطِق is the one given speech — the Prophet who voices the revealed law — set against the silent one who keeps and interprets its inner meaning.
فلك (orbit): from the root ف-ل-ك, tied to roundness and turning; the same root names the whirl of a spindle. A فَلَك is a revolving celestial sphere, named for the circling motion that never rests.

إمام (imam): from the root أ-م-م, to intend or head toward — the same root that gives أَمَام, "in front." An إِمَام is the one at the front, whom others face and follow, going ahead of them on the way.

notes.body:
The Will (الْإِرَادَة) is not Allah weighing a choice the way we weigh ours, turning a matter over until we decide. It is **the single, effortless turning by which He wills a thing into being** — no hesitation, no before-and-after in Him. When the Master sets "time" between the air and Allah and calls it the time of the Will, he points to the sheer moment of that turning, the instant of the command كن, "Be."

The trap is to hear "time" and picture a clock. **Ordinary time is a measure of change** — the sun moving, a shadow lengthening, a heartbeat. It needs created, moving things to measure, so it cannot run before creation; it is born with the world, not ahead of it.

The time of the Will only shares the name. It measures nothing created, because nothing created is yet there. It is not the ticking of the spheres but the "when" of an act — every act has its moment, and the Will's moment is the Word كن.

Consider striking a match in the dark. There is the instant of the strike, and then the flame that burns and can be timed. We cannot measure the strike by the flame's clock, for before the strike there is no flame to tick. **The strike is what starts the flame's time; it does not belong to that time.**

So the time of the Will "precedes" the air not by sitting earlier on a line — there is no line yet — but by standing nearer to Allah, above even the greatest created likeness. And it is the time *of* creation because it is the moment the Command is uttered, where willing and being are one breath:

> إِنَّمَا أَمْرُهُ إِذَا أَرَادَ شَيْئًا أَنْ يَقُولَ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ
>
> His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it "Be," and it is.
>
> Ya-Sin 36:82

Here the willing (أَرَادَ) and the "Be" (كُنْ) are not two steps with an interval between them. The Will and its command are one act, and its "time" is that act's own instant — the threshold at which the hidden passes into the made.
notes.anchor: It is the time of the Will
notes.quote: It is the time of the Will
etymology: إِرَادَة (will): from the root ر-و-د, whose sense is to go to and fro seeking — a رَائِد is the scout sent ahead to find pasture and water. Will, then, is the soul's seeking-out and settling upon a thing; Allah's Will is that turning without any lack, His pure inclining toward what shall be.

مَشِيئَة (will): from the root ش-ي-أ, the very root of شَيْء, "a thing." To will (شَاءَ) is, in its own letters, to make a thing be a thing — so the Will is the granting of reality to what was nothing, the point where a bare possibility is given its thing-hood.

كُنْ (be): the command form of كَانَ, "to be," from the root ك-و-ن — the same root as كَوْن, "existence," and الْكَوْن, "the cosmos." The single word كُنْ therefore already carries the whole created order within its letters: to say "Be" is to open being itself.

وَقْت (time): from the root و-ق-ت, a bounded and appointed measure — from it comes مِيقَات, the fixed time set for a rite. A وَقْت is never bare duration but a limit assigned to something, which fits a "time" that is nothing but the moment of the Command.
